title: Proteomic data: The Japanese Archipelago sheltered cave lions, not tigers, during the Late Pleistocene
projectDescription: Lions and tigers, as dominant apex predators, likely became competitors when lions expanded from Africa into Eurasia approximately one million years ago (Ma), forming a lion–tiger transition belt from the Middle East through Central Asia to the Russian Far East. At the easternmost edge of this zone, the Japanese Archipelago has long been considered a Late Pleistocene tiger refugium, supported by large felid subfossils traditionally attributed to tigers (Panthera tigris), though their taxonomic identity remained unresolved. To clarify the origin, evolutionary history, and biogeography of Japan’s Pleistocene felids, we analyzed 26 ancient specimens previously assumed to be tigers. Using mitochondrial and nuclear genome hybridization capture and sequencing, paleoproteomics, Bayesian molecular dating, and radiocarbon dating, we found that all ancient Japanese “tiger” remains yielding molecular data were, unexpectedly, cave lions (Panthera spelaea). One specimen was radiocarbon dated to 31,060 ± 190 BP. These cave lions likely dispersed to the Japanese Archipelago between ~72.7 and 37.5 thousand years ago (ka), when a land bridge connected northern Japan to the mainland during the Last Glacial Period. Our findings challenge the long-held view that tigers once took refuge in Japan, showing instead that cave lions were widespread in northeast Asia during this period and were the Panthera lineage that colonized Japan, reaching even its southwestern regions despite habitats previously thought to favor tigers.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Palaeoproteomic analysis was conducted to assess whether the endogenous protein sequence recovered from ancient specimens contained diagnostic variants characteristic of lions or tigers. Protein extraction from GMNH0031 was conducted in a dedicated ancient biomolecule facility at the Globe Institute, University of Copenhagen, using two established methods. First, a filter-aided protocol was applied to 20 mg of bone, involving decalcification with 0.5 M EDTA for two days, filtration through a molecular weight cutoff filter (Amicon 3000 Da), denaturation, reduction, and alkylation at 80 °C for 2–4 hours in a buffer containing 2 M guanidine hydrochloride (Gu), 10 mM tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP), and 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (CAA), followed by sequential digestion with 0.2 μg Lys-C (1.5 h at 37 °C) and 0.8 μg trypsin (overnight at 37℃) after dilution of Gu to 0.6 M. The second method was a digestion-free protocol in which 5.5 mg of bone was dissolved in 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) at 4℃ for two days. Blank controls were processed in parallel to monitor for potential exogenous contamination.  To minimize potential biases arising from annotation or translation errors in public protein databases, we generated reference proteomes from taxonomically verified lions and tigers. Proteins were extracted from modern samples of a lion (NHMD-CN-887) and a tiger (NHMD-CN-1021) kept at the Natural History Museum of Denmark. Approximately 20 mg of bone powder from each specimen was incubated in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ambic) at 65℃ for 1 hour. Protein concentration was measured using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay, and 20 μg aliquots were taken for digestion. For samples subjected to elastase digestion, ambic was evaporated, and the sample was resuspended in 50 mM Tris-HCl, followed by overnight digestion at 37℃ with either 0.4 μg elastase or trypsin. The resultant peptide solutions from all methods were purified using in-house-made reversed-phase C18 StageTips composed of two stacked C18 membranes. Peptides were eluted from the StageTips and injected into a liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) at the Center for Protein Research, University of Copenhagen. Separation was performed on a 15 cm column packed with 1.9 μm C18 beads using an EASY-nLC 1000 system (Proxeon, Odense, Denmark) coupled to a Q Exactive HF-X hybrid Quadrupole–Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Germany) with a 77-minute gradient, following previously described parameters.
dataProcessingProtocol: Mass spectrometry raw files were processed using a two-step database search strategy to refine species-specific protein identification. First, trypsin-digested fractions from GMNH0031 were searched in MaxQuant (v2.6.3.0) using a “specific” digestion mode against a merged database comprising complete modern lion and tiger proteomes downloaded from NCBI (May 2025). Similarly, the reference datasets from modern lion and tiger bones were searched against their respective species-specific databases.  In the second step, a reduced protein database was constructed, consisting of lion and tiger proteins (n = 70) identified in the first search with at least two razor and unique peptides. For each identified protein, homologous sequences from both species were included, even if the protein was detected in only one species. All ancient and modern fractions were then re-searched using an “unspecific” digestion mode against this reduced database. The results of the second search formed the basis for downstream analysis.
